provenance.notes: Mech family batch, quote archetype. Big tickets with regional players dominating ads, so copy leans on owner-led inspections and honest 'not every crack' advice. Warranty terms and engineer requirements stay bracketed; no pier system brands. Ranges are planning figures.

pageStructurePlus.section: Foundation warning signs: cosmetic or structural
pageStructurePlus.contains: Stair-step cracks in brick, doors that stick or won't latch, sloping floors, gaps at window frames, drywall cracks at corners, and which of these are usually cosmetic
pageStructurePlus.why: Homeowners panic at the first crack. The company that says honestly when it's cosmetic earns the inspection when it isn't.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Steel push piers, helical piers and pressed concrete pilings, how each is installed, which soils and house weights suit each, and how many piers a job might need
pageStructurePlus.why: Buyers get three quotes with three different pier types. A plain comparison makes your recommendation make sense.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Sagging floors over a crawlspace, shims and adjustable supports, rotted sill plates and beams, crawlspace moisture, and access through the skirting
pageStructurePlus.why: Older pier and beam homes need different work from slabs. Owners of those homes look for a company that clearly knows crawlspaces.

pageStructurePlus.section: Engineer's report, permit and repair letter
pageStructurePlus.contains: When an independent structural engineer is involved, the permit, the post-repair engineer's letter and how those documents help at resale, with bracketed local requirements
pageStructurePlus.why: Foundation work affects a home sale. Showing the paperwork trail reassures buyers that the repair will hold up to an inspector.

pageStructurePlus.section: Transferable warranty and selling the house
pageStructurePlus.contains: Bracketed warranty terms the owner supplies, how a transfer to a buyer works, what to hand the buyer's inspector, and disclosure documents
pageStructurePlus.why: Many foundation calls come right before a sale. A clear warranty-transfer page is often the deciding factor for sellers and their agents.

openers.angle: No site behind the map pin
openers.line: {Business Name} has solid foundation repair reviews on the map but no website. When someone finds a crack in the brick, the regional ad companies are all they see.
openers.hook: Open their Maps listing and confirm there is no Website button. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: The foundation repair site that pin could open: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your listing points to Facebook. A homeowner staring at a sloping kitchen floor wants to know if it's serious and book an inspection, not scroll through pier photos.
openers.hook: Tap their Website link and confirm it lands on Facebook. Note the latest foundation job.
openers.linkLine: A foundation page built for a worried homeowner: {demo-link}

openers.line: The foundation repair site on your profile has an old copyright year and a form that errors. For a job this big, buyers read a neglected site as a company that might not be around for the warranty.
openers.hook: Open the site and look for an old year, a host banner or a dead form. Note which one you found.
openers.linkLine: Same foundation company, current and sharp on a phone: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your foundation before-and-after shots don't load properly on my phone. That's the proof that sells a pier job, and most people are looking from a phone in the hallway.
openers.hook: Only if they have a site. Load the gallery on a phone and note what breaks. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: Your foundation gallery rebuilt for a phone: {demo-link}

openers.line: There's no way to request a foundation inspection from {Business Name} without phoning. People notice the cracks on a Sunday and want to send the address and a few shots.
openers.hook: Check the listing, social pages and any site for a form. If there is none, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: A foundation inspection request with a crack upload: {demo-link}

openers.angle: Not every crack is a problem
openers.line: The regional companies treat every hairline crack as an emergency. A page from {Business Name} that honestly says which cracks are cosmetic would make you the foundation company people trust.
openers.hook: Look for posts or reviews where they told someone a crack was fine. Quote it if you find it.
openers.linkLine: An honest foundation warning signs page: {demo-link}

openers.line: One of your reviews says you told them they didn't need piers yet and to fix the gutters first. That review is worth more than any ad, and it's buried on the map.
openers.hook: Read their reviews and copy one phrase about honesty, a pier job or level floors. Quote it back if they reply.
openers.linkLine: Those foundation reviews beside the inspection form: {demo-link}

openers.line: In a dry summer the clay soil around {City} shrinks and the new foundation cracks appear. The company that's easy to find that month books the inspections.
openers.hook: Use this in mid to late summer or during a dry spell. Name the season in the reply.
openers.linkLine: Ready before the dry-season foundation calls: {demo-link}

openers.line: Lots of foundation calls come when a buyer's inspector flags the slab days before closing. If your phone goes to voicemail that week, the seller's agent calls the next name.
openers.hook: Call their listed number after hours or check how fast they answer messages. If it's slow, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: A foundation request built for closing deadlines: {demo-link}

openers.line: Saw you're hiring for your foundation crew. Pier work is hard and heavy, and good hands pick the company that looks steady and well run.
openers.hook: Only if they posted a hiring note or story. Note the date of the post.
openers.linkLine: A foundation company page with a careers section: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your reviews mention foundation jobs in towns around {City}, but nothing tells someone in {Neighborhood} you work there. Owners search the town plus 'foundation repair'.
openers.hook: Find towns named in reviews or posts. Use the furthest one.
openers.linkLine: A foundation repair page for each town you cover: {demo-link}

openers.line: If {Business Name} offers payments on foundation work, put it on a page. A pier job is a number people need to see split up before they let anyone inspect.
openers.hook: Only if they mention financing somewhere: a post, a review, the truck. If not, skip this angle.
openers.linkLine: Foundation payment options, explained before the inspection: {demo-link}

openers.line: Foundation buyers worry about resale. A page showing that {Business Name} works with engineers and offers a transferable warranty answers the question the regional ads skip.
openers.hook: Look for any mention of engineers or warranty transfers. Never state a warranty term they haven't published.
openers.linkLine: Engineer's letter and warranty on one foundation page: {demo-link}

openers.line: It sounds like a lot of your foundation work comes from realtors and inspectors. If one of them starts sending sellers to a bigger outfit, that pipeline dries up.
openers.hook: Look for reviews mentioning a realtor, an inspection or a home sale. Quote it back.
openers.linkLine: Where a realtor's foundation referral would land: {demo-link}

openers.line: That {specific recent job} you posted is clean foundation work, piers set tidy and the yard put back. A homeowner should see that before any regional ad.
openers.hook: Pick their newest posted job and name it: slab piers, crawlspace supports or wall repair, and the town if tagged.
openers.linkLine: That foundation job, front and centre: {demo-link}

objections.objection: The big regional companies own the ads. I can't compete.
objections.handler: "Not on ad spend. On honesty and the owner showing up, yes. People who've had a hard-sell inspection search for a second opinion, and this site is built for them."

objections.objection: Most of my work comes from realtors and inspectors.
objections.handler: "Then the warranty transfer and engineer's letter pages are for them. Agents send sellers a link and you look like the safe choice."

objections.objection: I can't price foundation work online.
objections.handler: "We won't. The site explains how you quote, asks for shots of the cracks, and you price it after the inspection."

objections.objection: I don't want calls about every hairline crack.
objections.handler: "The warning signs page tells people which cracks are usually cosmetic, so those owners sort themselves out and the real ones book."

objections.objection: My nephew is working on a site.
objections.handler: "Good. If he wants the inspection form and the pier comparison, I'll hand them over. If it stalls, the offer stands."
"{Build Range}. For you, about {Build Price}, because it's an inspection form, a gallery and the warning signs and pier pages. One foundation job covers it many times."

bullets: Peg the build to a sliver of one pier job. Foundation owners think in piers and jobs, not pages.
The inspection request with crack upload is the core; price it as its own line.
Quote slab, pier and beam and wall repair pages separately; buyers search each differently.
Never publish a warranty term, pier count or engineer requirement the owner hasn't supplied; bracket it.
Before-and-after galleries are worth real money here; price by job count, not page count.
Don't compete with regional ad budgets. Scope for honesty, documents and local proof instead.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "License my foundation template with the crack upload form, pier comparison and warranty transfer page built."
